memories.content: The user renewed their local library membership in October 2024.
On an evening walk, the user saw an unlit street and took a detour along a main road.
On a day the user chose a well-lit pedestrian route, the walk took 12 minutes longer than usual.
On a day the user sat by the library window, they heard vehicle noise with every page they read.
On the next visit, the user sat farther inside and did not move for an hour.
The user wrote the due date of a borrowed book on paper and then lost the paper.
After entering the due date on their phone, the user saw a reminder the day before and put the book in their bag.
Library staff expect a person requesting a replacement membership card to bring identity-verification material.
Check recent lighting and pedestrian conditions before proposing an evening walking route.
The local agent can compare past reasons for detours but cannot directly observe current lighting and pedestrian conditions.
The user keeps a portable fan charger on a living-room shelf.
On a hot day, the user worked with only the window open and lost focus in the afternoon.
In the room where the user closed the curtains the next morning, the temperature rose less.
The user took the portable fan out without charging it, and it turned off after an hour.
Before the next outing, the user charged it the night before and used the fan throughout the trip.
On a hot weekend, the user was eating lunch in their father's yard and moved indoors.
When the user returned to the yard in the evening, shade and wind led them to stay another hour.
The user's father prefers to move an outdoor meal to the evening rather than proceed at midday when the temperature is high.
The local agent can compare past responses to heat but cannot know the current felt temperature without an indoor temperature record.
A room with a west-facing window can warm rapidly in the late afternoon.

analysis.overview: The frames cover separate domains: the reference records library use and evening-route safety, while the compared frame records heat management, portable-fan preparation, and outdoor-meal timing. No claims address the same operational policy closely enough to form a cross-frame relation.

relations.reason: This is independently useful reference-side membership history with no compared-side counterpart.
relations.summary: The user renewed a local library membership in October 2024.

relations.reason: These reference-side observations jointly describe the safety and time tradeoff of choosing better-lit evening routes; the compared frame contains no claim about walking routes.
relations.summary: The user avoided an unlit street, and a well-lit pedestrian route was observed to add twelve minutes.

relations.reason: These reference-side observations split one useful claim about how library seating location affected distraction and persistence, without a compared-side counterpart.
relations.summary: Window seating exposed the user to persistent vehicle noise, while sitting farther inside supported an uninterrupted hour.

relations.reason: These reference-side events jointly describe the relative reliability of two due-date tracking methods; the compared frame does not address borrowed-item reminders.
relations.summary: A paper due-date note was lost, whereas a phone reminder prompted the user to pack the borrowed book the day before it was due.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful reference-side procedural expectation with no compared-side analogue.
relations.summary: Library staff expect identity-verification material for a replacement membership-card request.

relations.reason: These reference-side claims split one operational constraint on proposing an evening walking route; the compared frame addresses heat assessment instead.
relations.summary: Evening-route proposals require recent lighting and pedestrian-condition information because the local agent can compare past detours but cannot directly observe current conditions.

relations.reason: This is independently useful compared-side location information with no reference-side counterpart.
relations.summary: The user keeps a portable fan charger on a living-room shelf.

relations.reason: These compared-side observations jointly describe indoor heat effects and a curtain-based response; the reference frame contains no indoor heat-management claim.
relations.summary: Working with only an open window on a hot day preceded lost afternoon focus, while closing the curtains the next morning limited the temperature rise.

relations.reason: These compared-side events split one useful claim about advance charging and portable-fan availability, without a reference-side counterpart.
relations.summary: An uncharged portable fan stopped after an hour, whereas charging it the night before allowed use throughout the next trip.

relations.reason: These compared-side memories jointly describe how heat, shade, wind, and family preference affect outdoor-meal timing; the reference frame has no corresponding meal policy.
relations.summary: Midday heat led the user to move indoors, while evening shade and wind supported a longer yard stay and aligned with the father’s preference to postpone hot-weather outdoor meals until evening.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful compared-side limitation on current heat assessment; the reference limitation concerns different environmental conditions and a different decision.
relations.summary: The local agent can compare past heat responses but cannot know the current felt temperature without an indoor temperature record.

relations.reason: This is independently useful compared-side information about room warming with no reference-side counterpart.
relations.summary: A room with a west-facing window can warm rapidly in the late afternoon.

reports.compared_only: Compared-only content covers indoor and outdoor heat responses, curtain use, portable-fan storage and charging, evening meal preferences, limits on assessing current temperature, and late-afternoon warming from west-facing windows.
reports.reference_only: Reference-only content covers membership, quieter library seating, due-date reminders, replacement-card verification, and the safety, delay, and current-condition checks involved in evening routes.
